title: Grace after meals
hookLine: four blessings: for food, for the land, for Jerusalem, for goodness

cards: In a lot of homes, grace comes first. The food is hot, everyone's hungry, someone says a few words, and the forks come out.
Jewish tradition does have a blessing before the meal: the short one over bread, thanking God who brings forth bread from the earth. But the big one, the one the Torah actually commands, comes after.
When the plates are empty and you're full and a little sleepy and nobody needs anything. That's exactly the moment the Torah picks.

teach.b: The source is in Deuteronomy: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." Eat, be satisfied, bless. In that order.
The rabbis read this as the command for Birkat HaMazon, the blessing for food. Its core is four blessings, and the Talmud, in Berakhot 48b, tells a story about where each came from.
The first, for food, thanks God who feeds the whole world. The tradition says Moses composed it when the manna began to fall in the desert.
The second, for the land, thanks God for the good land, and for the covenant and the Torah. Tradition credits Joshua, when the people entered the land.
The third asks for mercy on Jerusalem and its rebuilding; it's linked to David and Solomon, who made the city a capital and built the Temple. The fourth is later, and its story is sad.

After the Romans crushed the revolt at Betar, the dead lay unburied for a long time. When permission to bury them finally came, the sages at Yavneh added a blessing: to the One who is good and does good.
Good, that the bodies had not decayed. Good, that they could finally be buried. A blessing for goodness, born in grief.
Together they trace a whole history, from the desert to the land to the city to the ruins and back to gratitude. Many Jews sing it, especially on Shabbat, and it can take several minutes.
A full stomach turns into a short history lesson in thanks.

how: After a meal with bread, observant Jews recite Birkat HaMazon, usually from a small booklet called a bencher; on Shabbat and holidays it is often sung together at the table, with extra passages for the day.

games.why: the Torah picks the moment you're satisfied: that's when the main grace is said.

practice: Think back to the last thing you ate and walk the four blessings in your own way: the food and whoever grew and cooked it, the ground it came from, a place you love and want to see whole, and one good thing in your life, even if it came out of something hard.
If you pray, you can say the thanks to God.
